title: Arguments, theta roles and the Projection Principle (Oral Exam 1)
summary: What makes a phrase an argument or an adjunct; the three kinds of requirement a verb has (how many arguments, what category, what theta role); theta roles and theta grids; the Theta Criterion; the Projection Principle ('every head must have all of its requirements fulfilled') and the EPP; then the whole oral exam on the Projection Principle: the 2 to 3 minute explanation and ten practice sentences with X-bar trees.
sourceNote: Week 8 handout 'Arguments and adjuncts' (Dr. Nie): the definitions of argument, valency, selectional restrictions, the five theta roles and their examples, theta grids for place, dislike and scare, the Theta Criterion (7), the theta role hierarchy (8), the Projection Principle (1), expletives and the EPP (9) to (10), and the adjective and adverbial hierarchies. Oral exam format from the course's oral exam sign-up page. Trees follow the Week 6 phrase structure rules and the Week 7 X-bar handout (TP → DP T′, T′ → T VP, every nominal a DP, all three bar levels on every phrase).

sections.heading: Start here: verbs come with requirements

blocks.md: **The idea of this week.** A verb isn't just a word; it comes with a list of **requirements**. *Laugh* needs one participant, *eat* two, *put* three, *snow* none. The sentence has to supply exactly what the verb asks for. This week names those requirements (theta roles, theta grids) and the principle that enforces them: the **Projection Principle**.

steps.title: Theta Criterion
steps.sub: one role per argument, one argument per role

steps.title: Projection Principle + EPP
steps.sub: every requirement fulfilled; every clause has a subject

blocks.md: **Why it matters** This is your Oral Exam 1 topic (Thursday Oct 15, 12:00, CL 491). It's also the reason the trees from Weeks 6 and 7 look the way they do: the verb's requirements decide which phrases are complements and which are adjuncts.

sections.heading: Arguments and the three kinds of requirement

blocks.body: An **obligatory participant** of the verb. Each verb has requirements on the number and type of arguments it takes (its **selectional restrictions**).
An **optional** phrase the verb doesn't ask for: time, manner, extra location. You can drop it, and you can stack as many as you like.

rows: laugh, smile, sleep, arrive, fall, drift, rise
hit, build, defeat, praise, eat, create, like, watch
blocks.title: Number: English verbs allow 0 to 3 arguments

columns: Handout example (✓ fine, # odd or bad)
rows: *give* allows DP PP and DP DP: I gave [a book] [to George] ✓ · I gave [George] [a book] ✓. *place* allows only DP PP: # I placed [the table] [a book]
*give*'s PP must be an animate Recipient: # I gave a book to George's lap. *place*'s PP must be an inanimate Location: # I placed a book on George
blocks.title: The three requirements a verb has

blocks.body: Verbs that share the same requirements form a **subtype** (subcategory): *give* and *hand* (DP DP or DP PP), *place* and *put* (DP PP Location only).

blocks.prompt: Is 'in the kitchen' an argument or an adjunct in (a) 'Sam put the bowl in the kitchen' and (b) 'Sam ate in the kitchen'?
blocks.answer: (a) **Argument**: *put* requires a Location (# Sam put the bowl). (b) **Adjunct**: *eat* doesn't need a place (Sam ate is fine).

sections.heading: Theta roles: who does what to whom

blocks.md: **Grammatical relations vs theta roles.** 'Subject' and 'object' describe a phrase's role in the **sentence**, so they change when the sentence changes. **Theta roles** describe its role relative to the **verb**, so they stay the same.

columns: Passive: They were punched by her.
blocks.title: Same roles, different grammatical relations

rows: the initiator or doer of an action
*Rosa* danced all night · The cats were chased *by Zeno*
the entity that undergoes an action, is perceived or is experienced
Victor threw *the ball* · *The building* collapsed onto the ground
the entity that receives a theme; with verbs of transfer of possession
Michelle handed *Lee* a red pen · *Carlos* was gifted an office plant
the place where an action or state occurs
She quickly crossed *the street* · José slid the bag *under the table*
the entity that perceives an event or state
*Anna* noticed the train · The rabid dog scared *my poor cats*
blocks.title: The five major theta roles

blocks.body: Reading the role off the position. In 'The building collapsed', the subject is a **Theme** (it undergoes the collapse; nobody did it). In 'The rabid dog scared my poor cats', the Experiencer is the **object**. Ask what the phrase **does in the event**, not where it sits.

blocks.prompt: Give the theta roles in 'Anna noticed the train'.

sections.heading: Theta grids and the Theta Criterion

blocks.body: A verb's requirements written down: the **number**, **category** and **theta role** of each argument, as slots x, y, z. Arguments can be DPs or PPs.

blocks.title: Handout theta grids
blocks.body:
place  (Carly placed the briefcase on the table)
  x: DP Agent      y: DP Theme          z: PP Location
     Carly           the briefcase         on the table

dislike  (The boss disliked the strong smell)
  x: DP Experiencer   y: DP Theme
     the boss            the strong smell

scare  (Horror movies scare Lisa)
  x: DP Theme      y: DP Experiencer
     horror movies    Lisa
**Every theta role is assigned to one and only one argument. Every argument is assigned one and only one theta role.** No empty slots, no double roles, no extra arguments with no role.
Roles usually line up in this order: **Agent, Experiencer > Theme, Recipient > Location**. The higher role tends to be the subject. Exception: *scare* (Theme > Experiencer).

rows: the Location role has no argument (role left unassigned)
# Carly placed the briefcase on the table the book.
*the book* gets no role (argument with no role)
the Theme role has no argument
blocks.title: Theta Criterion violations

blocks.prompt: Write the theta grid for *throw* in 'Victor threw the ball'.

blocks.body: **Every head must have all of its requirements fulfilled.** (Dr. Nie's handout (1).) A head's requirements are its number of arguments, their categories and their theta roles: its theta grid. The sentence, and so the tree, must contain a phrase for every one of them.

blocks.md: **Why it's called 'projection'.** The requirements live in the head (in its lexical entry), and they **project** up into the structure: the head's grid decides what has to appear around it in the tree. The tree is the head's requirements made visible.

columns: Where it goes in the X-bar tree
rows: **complement**: sister of V, daughter of the lowest V′
external argument (the x slot, usually the highest role)
**adjunct**: sister of a V′ (one V′ per adjunct)
blocks.title: The Projection Principle decides where every phrase goes

blocks.caption: Carly placed the briefcase on the table. All three of *place*'s requirements are in the tree: Carly in Spec,TP, the briefcase and on the table as complements of V. Click the lowest V′: V and both its complements.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Carly]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V placed] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N briefcase]]]]] [PP [P′ [P on] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N table]]]]]]]]]]]

rows: # I placed the table a book.
**category**: place wants DP PP, not DP DP
# I placed a book on George.
**theta role**: place's PP must be an inanimate Location
**number**: laugh has one slot; the joke has no role (Theta Criterion too)
blocks.title: Four ways to break the Projection Principle

blocks.body: Putting an argument PP as an adjunct (or the reverse). In 'put the keys in the drawer before dinner', *in the drawer* is put's Location: complement, sister of V. *before dinner* isn't in the grid: adjunct, sister of V′. Two PPs, two different positions, decided by the grid.

blocks.md: **The problem the Projection Principle can't solve alone.** Zero-argument predicates (*snow*, *rain*, *seem*) have no requirements, so the Projection Principle asks for nothing. Yet English still needs a subject: 'It snowed yesterday', never just 'Snowed yesterday'.

blocks.body: A subject that **doesn't mean or refer to anything**: *it* in 'It snowed yesterday' and 'It seems that horror movies scare Lisa', *there* in 'There appears to be a problem with our oven'. It gets **no theta role**.
**Every clause must have a subject.** (Handout (10).) The structural position is the **specifier of TP**.

blocks.caption: Handout task: 'It snowed yesterday' in X-bar. *It* sits in Spec,TP to satisfy the EPP (no theta role, since snow has none to give). *yesterday* is an adjunct: sister of V′.

blocks.md: **Projection Principle vs EPP in one line each:** the Projection Principle says every head gets **everything it asks for**; the EPP says every clause gets **a subject, even if no head asked for one**. The expletive is how English satisfies the EPP without breaking the Theta Criterion.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md: Adjuncts aren't required, but they still come in a preferred order.

blocks.title: Adjective hierarchy (fairly rigid, possibly universal; subjectivity predicts the order)
Adverbial hierarchy (freer; both AdvPs and PPs act as adverbials)

blocks.prompt: Why is 'a wooden old chair' odd?
blocks.answer: Age comes before material in the adjective hierarchy: **an old wooden chair**.

blocks.title: How the 10 points break down (Thu Oct 15, 12:00, CL 491, whiteboard)

blocks.md:
**Definition.** The Projection Principle says that every head must have all of its requirements fulfilled. A verb, for example, comes with requirements on its arguments: how many it takes, what syntactic category each one is, and what theta role each one plays. We write those requirements as a theta grid, and the Projection Principle says the sentence has to fulfill every one of them.

**Example.** Take place, as in 'Carly placed the briefcase on the table.' Its theta grid has three slots: a DP Agent, a DP Theme and a PP Location. Carly, the briefcase and on the table fill them. If I drop one, 'Carly placed the briefcase', the sentence is bad because place's Location requirement isn't fulfilled. The category matters too: 'I placed the table a book' is bad because place wants DP PP, not DP DP. And the role matters: 'I placed a book on George' is odd because the PP has to be an inanimate Location.

**What it solves.** It explains why some phrases are obligatory and others aren't. Anything in the head's grid is an argument and has to be there: in the tree, the internal arguments are complements, sisters of V, and the external argument is the subject in Spec,TP. Anything that isn't in the grid, like 'yesterday' or 'in the morning', is an adjunct: it's optional, I can stack as many as I want, and it attaches to V′. So the Projection Principle tells me where each phrase goes before I draw anything.

**What it raises.** Some verbs have no requirements at all, like snow. The Projection Principle asks for nothing there, but English still says 'It snowed', with a subject that means nothing. So we also need the Extended Projection Principle: every clause must have a subject. The expletive 'it' fills the subject position without getting a theta role, which also keeps the Theta Criterion happy.

**Timing:** read at a calm pace, this script is about 2.5 minutes. You can bring it as notes, but practice it until you only glance at the bold words. For the examples, **write them on the whiteboard as you talk**: the theta grid for *place* with x, y, z, and the three starred sentences. Writing is what makes it look fluent.

blocks.title: If she asks you to elaborate
blocks.body:
"What's a theta grid?"  → the verb's requirements written down: number, category and theta role of each argument.
"How is that different from the Theta Criterion?"  → the Projection Principle says the requirements must be fulfilled; the Theta Criterion says the matching is one-to-one (one role per argument, one argument per role).
"Why do we need the EPP?"  → snow has no requirements but 'It snowed' still needs a subject: an expletive with no role.
"Do only verbs have requirements?"  → no, every head: possessive 's needs a possessor and a possessed noun; a preposition needs its DP object.

sections.heading: Oral Exam 1: the practical, step by step

blocks.md: No notes here, so learn these six steps by heart. They also earn the 2 points for 'demonstrate and explain your approach before drawing a tree': **say each step out loud** as you do it.

columns: What to do (and say out loud)
rows: Underline every verb (and any other head that selects, like possessive 's). Say what kind of verb it is: zero, one, two or three arguments.
For the main verb: x, y, z with category and theta role (DP Agent, DP Theme, PP Location…). Say it out loud: 'place needs a DP Agent, a DP Theme and a PP Location.'
Point to the phrase that fills each slot. Use the Theta Criterion: one role per argument, one argument per role. If there's no subject role (snow, rain, seem), the subject is an expletive (EPP).
4. Everything left over is an adjunct
Any phrase not in a grid (time, manner, place words the verb doesn't need) is an adjunct. Prove it: it can be dropped, and you could stack another.

TP → DP T′ (subject in Spec,TP), T′ → T VP (T = PAST, PRES or an auxiliary like will). Complements: sisters of V under the lowest V′. Adjuncts: one new V′ each (V′ → V′ AdvP/PP, or AdvP V′ on the left).
Every phrase has all three levels (XP, X′, X); every nominal is a DP. Then check: is every requirement in the grid filled exactly once? That's the Projection Principle, verified on your own tree.
blocks.title: The six steps (memorize the left column)

blocks.md: **A one-line mnemonic for the six steps:** *Verbs, Grid, Match, Leftovers, Place, Check*.

blocks.caption: (1) Carly placed the briefcase on the table.  Theta grid of **place**: DP Agent = *Carly*; DP Theme = *the briefcase*; PP Location = *on the table*. No adjuncts. place needs three things, so all three must be in the tree: Carly in Spec,TP (the external argument), the briefcase and on the table as complements, sisters of V. Drop the PP and place is left unfulfilled: *Carly placed the briefcase.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Carly]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V placed] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N briefcase]]]]] [PP [P′ [P on] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N table]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (2) The boss disliked the strong smell.  Theta grid of **dislike**: DP Experiencer = *the boss*; DP Theme = *the strong smell*. No adjuncts. dislike has two requirements: an Experiencer (the boss, subject) and a Theme (the strong smell, complement). 'strong' is not in dislike's grid at all: it's an adjunct inside the NP, sister of N′.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N boss]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V disliked] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj strong]]] [N′ [N smell]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (3) Horror movies scare Lisa.  Theta grid of **scare**: DP Theme = *horror movies*; DP Experiencer = *Lisa*. No adjuncts. scare's requirements are a Theme and an Experiencer, in that order: the exception to the theta hierarchy (Experiencer usually comes first). The Projection Principle doesn't care about the order of roles, only that both are filled, once each.

(4) It snowed yesterday.  Theta grid of **snow**: none (zero arguments). Adjuncts: *yesterday*. snow has NO requirements (a zero-argument predicate), so the Projection Principle asks for nothing. But English still demands a subject: that's the EPP. 'It' is an expletive: it fills Spec,TP but gets no theta role. 'yesterday' is an adjunct (sister of V′).

(5) Michelle handed Lee a red pen.  Theta grid of **hand**: DP Agent = *Michelle*; DP Recipient = *Lee*; DP Theme = *a red pen*. No adjuncts. hand takes DP DP complements here (like give): Recipient first, then Theme. All three requirements fulfilled: Michelle (subject), Lee and a red pen (both complements of V).

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Michelle]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V handed] [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Lee]]]]] [DP [D′ [D a] [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj red]]] [N′ [N pen]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (6) The tired students laughed loudly in the hallway.  Theta grid of **laugh**: DP Agent = *the tired students*. Adjuncts: *loudly*, *in the hallway*. laugh has one requirement, filled by the subject. Everything after the verb is NOT in its grid, so loudly and in the hallway are adjuncts: each gets its own V′ (V′ → V′ AdvP, then V′ → V′ PP), and the lowest V′ has the verb alone.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj tired]]] [N′ [N students]]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V′ [V′ [V laughed]] [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv loudly]]]] [PP [P′ [P in] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N hallway]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (7) My roommate will put the keys in the drawer before dinner.  Theta grid of **put**: DP Agent = *my roommate*; DP Theme = *the keys*; PP Location = *in the drawer*. Adjuncts: *before dinner*. Two PPs, two different jobs. in the drawer is put's Location requirement (a complement, sister of V). before dinner is not in put's grid (an adjunct, sister of V′). 'will' is in T.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D my] [NP [N′ [N roommate]]]]] [T′ [T will] [VP [V′ [V′ [V put] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N keys]]]]] [PP [P′ [P in] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N drawer]]]]]]]] [PP [P′ [P before] [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N dinner]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (8) Rosa sent a letter to her grandmother on Tuesday.  Theta grid of **send**: DP Agent = *Rosa*; DP Theme = *a letter*; PP Recipient = *to her grandmother*. Adjuncts: *on Tuesday*. send's Recipient can be a PP (to her grandmother), like give. on Tuesday is time, not in send's grid: adjunct. The test: 'Rosa sent a letter to her grandmother' is complete; 'Rosa sent a letter on Tuesday' still needs the recipient understood.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Rosa]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V′ [V sent] [DP [D′ [D a] [NP [N′ [N letter]]]]] [PP [P′ [P to] [DP [D′ [D her] [NP [N′ [N grandmother]]]]]]]] [PP [P′ [P on] [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Tuesday]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (9) She quickly crossed the street.  Theta grid of **cross**: DP Agent = *she*; DP Location = *the street*. Adjuncts: *quickly*. cross's Location is a DP here (the street), straight from the handout's (5a): a Location doesn't have to be a PP. quickly is an adjunct on the left: V′ → AdvP V′.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D she]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv quickly]]] [V′ [V crossed] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N street]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (10) The chef's assistant ate the cake.  Theta grid of **eat**: DP Agent = *the chef's assistant*; DP Theme = *the cake*. No adjuncts. Heads other than verbs have requirements too: the possessive 's needs a possessor (the chef, its specifier) and a possessed noun (assistant, its complement). eat's two requirements: the whole DP the chef's assistant (Agent) and the cake (Theme).

params.bracket: [TP [DP [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N chef]]]]] [D′ [D 's] [NP [N′ [N assistant]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V ate] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N cake]]]]]]]]]

blocks.body: Forgetting the bar levels. Dr. Nie's trees have **all three levels on every phrase**, even a lone word: [DP [D′ [D it]]], [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv yesterday]]]. And every nominal is a DP (a name gets an empty D: [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP Carly]]]).
